title: RAG threat model and OWASP LLM Top 10 2025
summary: A threat model for RAG lists what you protect, who can write into each stage and where text crosses a trust boundary, then maps those risks to the OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 ids.
useIf: You are starting a RAG design review and need a shared vocabulary for what can go wrong.
avoidIf: You already have a threat model and need a specific control. Jump to the access control or defence topics.

explain.md: The model can only leak what retrieval hands it, and it will follow any instruction that arrives inside that text. A RAG threat model therefore starts with two questions: **who can write into each stage** and **what can each stage read or send out**. Assets are the documents and their permissions, the embeddings, the system prompt, the caller's identity and tokens, and every tool the model can call.

explain.title: Where text crosses a trust boundary
explain.alt: Writers feed ingestion and the index. A caller's question and the retrieved chunks both enter the prompt. The model output reaches a client and tools, which are the exit points.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  W[Writers: staff, customers, web] --> I[Ingestion]
  I --> X[(Index)]
  C[Caller question] --> R[Retrieval]
  X --> R
  R --> P[Prompt]
  P --> M[Model]
  M --> O[Output renderer]
  M --> T[Tools]

explain.md: Every arrow that carries text written by someone other than the caller is an attack path. Run the model in three passes:

items: List the assets and who may see each one.
List the writers at each stage and mark the untrusted ones.
List the exits: the output renderer, tools, logs and caches.

explain.md: The OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 names the risks that matter at each point [[r1]].

explain.title: Two neighbouring lists
explain.md: OWASP also published a Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (ASI01 to ASI10) on 2025-12-09 [[r3]], and MITRE ATLAS lists RAG techniques such as AML.T0064 and AML.T0070 [[r4]]. Do not confuse them with the LLM list.

whereToUse: Design reviews before a RAG assistant gets access to real documents
Interview answers that must show a layered view instead of one guard
Choosing which of the later topics to read first for your corpus and tools
Incident post-mortems: classify the leak by id and by stage

use: A new corpus mixes authors you do not fully trust
The assistant can call tools or render rich output
Several teams own different pipeline stages
avoid: You need an implementation recipe: use the topic for that control
The system has no retrieval and no tools, so most items drop out
You expect the list to be complete: it is a shared vocabulary, not a design
flips: The corpus is written only by vetted staff: weight LLM04 lower and LLM02 higher
The assistant gains a send or write tool: LLM06 and LLM01 move to the top

pitfalls.symptom: The review lists only prompt injection
pitfalls.cause: Treating RAG as a prompt problem
pitfalls.fix: Walk each stage: ingest, index, retrieve, prompt, output, tools

pitfalls.symptom: Everyone assumes the system prompt enforces access
pitfalls.cause: LLM07 is ignored: the prompt is not a secret or a control
pitfalls.fix: Move rules and secrets to code that runs outside the model

pitfalls.cause: No trigger on new sources or tools
pitfalls.fix: Re-run it whenever a writer, tool or output channel is added

scenarios.title: Read-only assistant over staff-written pages
scenarios.situation: An assistant answers questions over an internal wiki. Everyone with write access is an employee. The assistant has no tools and renders plain text. Documents carry per-team permissions.
unknowns: Who can edit pages, and can contractors?
Does the client render Markdown or fetch images?
scenarios.question: Which risk do you address first?

options.name: Add a prompt-injection classifier on every chunk
options.why: Cheap insurance against a careless or malicious edit.
options.tradeoff: Adds latency and false positives while the main exposure stays open.

options.name: Enforce the caller's permissions inside retrieval (LLM02, LLM08)
options.why: Authors are trusted and there is no outbound channel, so the realistic loss is a chunk reaching the wrong reader.
options.tradeoff: Needs ACL capture at ingest and a sync story.

options.name: Tell the model in the system prompt not to reveal restricted pages
options.why: The model is not an authorization layer and the prompt can be extracted or overridden.
options.tradeoff: Fine as a tone instruction, never as the access control.

flips.if: Anyone on the internet can edit a page
flips.then: Injection and poisoning rise to the top: add ingest review and spotlighting.

flips.if: The client renders images from model output
flips.then: Output handling (LLM05) joins the first tier.

scenarios.takeaway: Rank risks by who can write, what can leave and how much agency exists.

scenarios.title: Customer tickets in, email out
scenarios.situation: A support agent reads customer-submitted tickets, looks up account data and can send replies automatically. Volume is high and replies are sent without review.
unknowns: Can a reply include data from other accounts?
Is a human review step acceptable for some replies?
scenarios.question: How do you reduce the risk most?

options.name: Stack a classifier, spotlighting and a stricter prompt
options.why: Lowers attack success and is worth having.
options.tradeoff: All three are probabilistic, so a single bypass still reaches the channel.

options.name: Rely on one best-in-class input classifier
options.why: EchoLeak bypassed a production classifier as one link in its chain.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only when the agent cannot send or fetch anything.

options.name: Remove one leg: draft replies for human approval, or block account data in that session
options.why: Untrusted input, private data and an outbound channel together are the shape of EchoLeak-style exfiltration [[r10]] [[r6]].
options.tradeoff: Adds reviewer time or reduces automation.

flips.if: Replies go only to the ticket author and carry no account data
flips.then: The private data leg is gone and automation is fine.
Restrict the tool to templated replies and block free-text exfiltration paths.

scenarios.takeaway: When all three legs are present, design out a leg before adding guards.

quiz.q: Match each OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 id to its RAG shape.

pairs.r: A chunk the caller may not read reaches the prompt
Cross-tenant context leak in a shared vector store

quiz.explain: LLM02 is disclosure, LLM04 is poisoning of embedding data, LLM05 is unvalidated output handling such as Markdown that triggers fetches, and LLM08 covers vector store weaknesses including cross-context leaks.

quiz.q: A reviewer says RAG removes prompt injection risk because answers are grounded. What is the right reply?
options: Incorrect: OWASP says RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate prompt injection
Correct for indirect injection, incorrect for direct injection
quiz.explain: Retrieved text is itself an input channel. Indirect injection arrives through documents, so grounding adds an attack path instead of removing one.

flashcards.front: Which two questions start a RAG threat model?
flashcards.back: Who can write into each stage, and what can each stage read or send out. Then mark every point where someone else's text enters the prompt.

flashcards.front: Which OWASP LLM 2025 id covers cross-tenant leaks in a shared vector store?
flashcards.back: LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, alongside inversion and poisoning.

flashcards.front: Name the three legs of the Rule of Two.
flashcards.back: Untrustworthy inputs, access to sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally. Keep at most two in one session.
